content: Physical activity, including structured exercise programs, is considered an important component of routine care for individuals with cystic fibrosis (CF). This updated review aimed to evaluate the effects of physical activity interventions on various outcomes, including exercise capacity (measured by peak oxygen uptake), lung function (assessed by forced expiratory volume in one second, or FEV1), health-related quality of life (HRQoL), and other patient-relevant outcomes. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and quasi-RCTs that compared physical activity interventions of at least two weeks' duration to standard care (no physical activity intervention) in individuals with CF. A total of 24 parallel RCTs involving 875 participants were included. The studies varied widely in terms of participant age, disease severity, intervention duration, and supervision levels. Fourteen studies implemented training programs lasting up to six months, while ten studies extended beyond six months. Seven studies included a follow-up period (ranging from one to 12 months) during which participants were allowed to exercise without supervision. The findings suggest that physical activity interventions lasting longer than six months likely improve exercise capacity compared to no physical activity (mean difference [MD] 1.60, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.16 to 3.05; moderate-certainty evidence). However, the magnitude of improvement in exercise capacity was small, and the results were heterogeneous across studies. Physical activity interventions appeared to have little to no effect on lung function (FEV1 % predicted) (MD 2.41, 95% CI ‒0.49 to 5.31; low-certainty evidence) or HRQoL, including physical functioning (MD 2.19, 95% CI ‒3.42 to 7.80) and respiratory domain scores (MD ‒0.05, 95% CI ‒3.61 to 3.51; low-certainty evidence). One study involving 117 participants found no significant differences between the physical activity and control groups in the incidence of pulmonary exacerbations by six months (incidence rate ratio 1.28, 95% CI 0.85 to 1.94) or in the time to first exacerbation over 12 months (hazard ratio 1.34, 95% CI 0.65 to 2.80). Additionally, physical activity did not appear to affect diabetic control, as measured by blood glucose levels at one and two hours post-intervention (moderate-certainty evidence). There was no significant difference in the number of adverse events between groups over six months (odds ratio 6.22, 95% CI 0.72 to 53.40; low-certainty evidence). For outcomes assessed at other time points (up to six months or during follow-up periods without active intervention), the effects of physical activity were consistent with the findings described above. However, only three of the seven studies with follow-up periods reported on primary outcomes such as changes in exercise capacity and lung function, and only one study reported on HRQoL. These data should be interpreted cautiously due to the limited evidence. Overall, the certainty of evidence regarding the effects of physical activity interventions on exercise capacity, lung function, and HRQoL is considered low to moderate. While physical activity interventions lasting six months or longer likely improve exercise capacity, they appear to have little or no effect on lung function or HRQoL. Adverse effects of physical activity are rare, and there is no reason to discourage regular physical activity in individuals with CF. The benefits of incorporating physical activity into routine care may depend on the type and duration of the activity program, as well as individual preferences and barriers to participation. Further high-quality, adequately powered studies are needed to better understand the benefits of physical activity and exercise in individuals with CF, particularly in the context of advancements in CF treatment and care.
